title: Biological Membranes
scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT biochemistry lessons covering the declared outline sections. This release is implemented, not independently scientifically verified; it is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: The fluid mosaic model describes a dynamic lipid matrix with associated proteins. Components move laterally, subject to interactions and structural constraints.
The two leaflets can differ in lipid composition. Spontaneous movement of many phospholipid head groups across the hydrophobic core is slow without facilitating proteins.
Membrane proteins can have transport, receptor or anchoring roles. The model does not require every protein to diffuse freely without restriction.
Fluidity depends on temperature, tail composition and cholesterol. A schematic is an organizational model, not a fixed universal membrane composition.

steps.text: Integral proteins interact with the membrane interior; transmembrane proteins span the bilayer. Peripheral proteins associate with a surface or another protein.
Carbohydrate groups on plasma-membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids generally face the noncytosolic side, contributing to recognition and protection.
Cholesterol’s polar hydroxyl lies near head groups while its hydrophobic body associates with tails. A cartoon orientation is not an atom-resolved structural claim.
Removing a peripheral protein may require milder conditions than solubilizing an integral protein. Extraction behavior can suggest association but is not a full structure determination.

steps.text: Passive transport moves a solute down its electrochemical gradient. Facilitated diffusion uses a protein but does not by itself make transport active.
Primary active transport couples movement to an energy source such as ATP hydrolysis. Secondary active transport uses one solute gradient to drive another solute uphill.
An ion’s driving force combines concentration and electrical contributions. An unfavorable concentration difference alone does not establish the net electrochemical direction.
Osmosis describes water movement in response to effective osmotic gradients. Tonicity depends on nonpenetrating solutes and membrane properties, not total particle concentration alone.

steps.text: Specialized membranes support distinct functions through protein and lipid composition. Location matters when interpreting a transport or energetic pathway.
The inner mitochondrial membrane sustains the proton gradient used for oxidative phosphorylation and is selectively permeable. The outer membrane has different permeability properties.
Myelin electrically insulates portions of axons, supporting saltatory conduction between nodes. It does not replace the need for ion gradients or membrane channels.
Polarized epithelia position different transporters on apical and basolateral surfaces. A carrier’s location can determine net tissue-level transport.
